lessons.title: What Is Python & Setting Up Your Environment

slots.practicalActivity: Install Python 3 and a code editor (or confirm an existing install's version with python --version), create a new project folder, and write a one-line script that prints your name and today's date. Run it from the terminal, not just inside the editor, so you've confirmed the whole path from file to output works.
slots.deliverable: A working hello.py script, run successfully from the terminal.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a short script that stores a product name, quantity, and unit price as variables of the correct types, computes the line total, and prints a formatted summary line using an f-string (e.g. "3x Trail Runner GTX @ $129.99 = $389.97"). Then deliberately try an operation that mixes an int and a str to see the real TypeError, and fix it.
slots.deliverable: A script that prints one correctly formatted order-line summary, plus a one-sentence note on what caused the TypeError and how you fixed it.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a list of 5 product names (include at least one duplicate on purpose), then use a set to find the real distinct count. Use a tuple to represent one fixed (latitude, longitude) coordinate pair and explain in a comment why a tuple, not a list, is the right choice here.
slots.deliverable: A script printing both the raw list length and the deduplicated set count, with the tuple example and its justifying comment.

slots.practicalActivity: Model one real order record as a dictionary (order_id, customer_name, product, quantity, unit_price), then write a small function that takes that dict and returns the computed line total using the correct keys. Handle a missing key with .get() and a sensible default instead of letting it crash.
slots.deliverable: A function that correctly computes a line total from a dict-shaped order record, tested against at least 2 different records.

slots.practicalActivity: Given a small list of order dicts (reuse Lesson 5's shape), loop through them and print only the ones where quantity is 0 or negative — the exact kind of data-quality check a real ingestion script runs. Use an if/elif/else to label each remaining order 'small' (qty < 3) or 'bulk' (qty >= 3).
slots.deliverable: A script that correctly flags invalid-quantity orders and labels the valid ones small/bulk.

slots.practicalActivity: Refactor Lesson 4's line-total logic into a properly named, documented function with a docstring and type hints on its parameters and return value. Write 3 real calls to it with different inputs and print each result.
slots.deliverable: A documented, type-hinted compute_line_total() function, called successfully 3 times with different real inputs.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a function that applies an optional discount (default 0%) to a line total, called once with the default and once overriding it with a keyword argument. Then write a second function that validates an order record and returns both a boolean (is it valid) and a list of specific problems found — practicing returning multiple values instead of one combined value.
slots.deliverable: Two working functions: one with a working default/keyword-argument override, one returning a (bool, list) validation result.

slots.practicalActivity: Split your line-total and validation functions out of your main script into a separate helpers.py file, then import and call both from a new main script using import helpers. Confirm it still runs correctly after the split.
slots.deliverable: A two-file project (helpers.py + a main script importing it) that runs correctly end to end.

slots.practicalActivity: Given a list of order dicts, write one list comprehension that extracts just the product names, and one dict comprehension that maps order_id to line total. Compare the comprehension version against an equivalent for-loop version and note which reads more clearly.
slots.deliverable: Working comprehension versions of both extractions, plus a one-sentence comparison against the loop version.

slots.practicalActivity: Parse a real date string like "2026-01-13" into a datetime object with datetime.strptime, then compute how many days old that order is relative to today using datetime.now(). Format the result back out as a human-readable string like "13 days ago".
slots.deliverable: A function that takes an order-date string and returns a correct human-readable age, tested against 2 different real dates.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the course's real orders.csv dataset, open it with the csv module (not pandas yet) using a with block, read it row by row with csv.DictReader, and print the product name and quantity for every row where status is 'Shipped'. Then write a small log file recording how many rows you read and how many matched.
slots.deliverable: A script that correctly filters orders.csv by status using csv.DictReader, plus a log file recording the row counts.

slots.practicalActivity: Convert 5 real rows from orders.csv into a list of dictionaries and write them out as a JSON file with json.dump(). Then read that JSON file back in with json.load() and confirm the round-tripped data matches what you started with.
slots.deliverable: A real orders.json file produced from orders.csv, successfully read back and verified to match.

slots.practicalActivity: Wrap your CSV-reading code in a real try/except/finally: catch FileNotFoundError specifically (test it by pointing at a file that doesn't exist) and a generic Exception as a fallback, logging a clear message for each rather than letting the script crash with a raw traceback.
slots.deliverable: A script that fails gracefully with a clear logged message when the input file is missing, instead of crashing.

lessons.title: Calling a REST API With requests

slots.practicalActivity: Use the requests library to call the real, public GitHub API (e.g. GET https://api.github.com/repos/pandas-dev/pandas) with no authentication required, check response.status_code, and pull out 3 real fields from the JSON response (e.g. stargazers_count, open_issues_count, description).
slots.deliverable: A script that successfully calls the real GitHub API and prints 3 real fields from the live response.

lessons.title: Pagination & Rate Limits in Real APIs

slots.practicalActivity: Call the real GitHub API's contributors endpoint for a public repo with ?per_page=5 and follow the Link response header to fetch a second page. Check the X-RateLimit-Remaining response header and print it, so you've seen a real API's rate-limit signal, not just read about it.
slots.deliverable: A script that fetches 2 real pages of results from the GitHub API and prints the live rate-limit-remaining value.

lessons.title: Reading Data Into Pandas (CSV, JSON, Excel)

slots.practicalActivity: Load the real orders.csv into a DataFrame with pd.read_csv(), print df.shape and df.dtypes, and confirm the row count matches what you counted by hand in Lesson 11 (20 rows). Then load the orders.json file you created in Lesson 12 with pd.read_json() and confirm both loading paths produce a DataFrame with the same columns.
slots.deliverable: Confirmation (printed shape/dtypes) that both the CSV and JSON versions of the same data load into matching DataFrames.

slots.practicalActivity: On the real orders DataFrame, select just the product and quantity columns, then filter to orders where region is 'West' and status is 'Shipped' using boolean indexing with &. Confirm your filtered row count by counting matching rows in the raw CSV by eye.
slots.deliverable: A correctly filtered DataFrame (West region, Shipped status) with a row count you've manually verified against the source file.

slots.practicalActivity: Use df.isna().sum() to find the real missing customer_name on order 1005, and df[df['quantity'] < 0] to find the real negative-quantity row (order 1014). Decide and apply a real fix for each (e.g. flag or drop) rather than silently ignoring them, and print a before/after row count.
slots.deliverable: A cleaned DataFrame with both real data-quality issues (missing name, negative quantity) explicitly found and handled, plus a before/after row count.

slots.practicalActivity: Add a real line_total column to the orders DataFrame computed from quantity * unit_price, then use .apply() with a small function to label each row 'bulk' (quantity >= 3) or 'standard'. Verify 2 of the computed line totals by hand against the raw CSV numbers.
slots.deliverable: A DataFrame with a correct line_total column and a bulk/standard label column, with 2 values hand-verified.

slots.practicalActivity: Group the real orders DataFrame by region and compute total revenue (sum of line_total) per region, then group by product and compute total quantity sold per product. Identify, from the real numbers, which region has the highest revenue and which product sold the most units.
slots.deliverable: Two real groupby results (revenue by region, units by product), with the top region and top product named from the actual computed numbers.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a small second DataFrame mapping each real product name in orders.csv to a category (Footwear, Camping, Packs, Accessories — these already appear in the dataset), then merge it onto the orders DataFrame with pd.merge() on product, and confirm every order row now has a category with no nulls introduced by the join.
slots.deliverable: A merged DataFrame where every real order row has a correct category and no new nulls were introduced.

lessons.title: Running Queries & Loading Results Into Pandas

slots.practicalActivity: Using pyodbc, connect to your own SQL Server instance's real AdventureWorks2012 database (the same one used in this site's T-SQL Development course), then run a real query against Production.Product with pd.read_sql() and confirm the returned DataFrame's row count matches what SSMS shows for the same query.
slots.deliverable: A working Python connection to a real AdventureWorks2012 database, with a query result loaded into a DataFrame and row-count-verified against SSMS.

lessons.title: Writing Data Back to a Database

slots.practicalActivity: Create a new, small staging table in your own database (not a production AdventureWorks2012 table) and write your cleaned orders DataFrame into it with df.to_sql() or an explicit INSERT loop, then query it back to confirm every row landed correctly.
slots.deliverable: A real database table populated from your cleaned orders DataFrame, with a verification query confirming the row count matches.

slots.practicalActivity: Rewrite one of your earlier queries to accept a variable (e.g. a region name) two ways: first with unsafe f-string interpolation, then with a proper parameterized query using ? placeholders. Explain in a comment exactly what a malicious region value like "' OR '1'='1" would do to the unsafe version.
slots.deliverable: A parameterized query proven to work, plus a written explanation of the specific SQL injection risk in the unsafe version it replaced.

slots.practicalActivity: Rebuild Lesson 22's database connection using SQLAlchemy's create_engine() instead of raw pyodbc, and run the same query through pd.read_sql() against the engine. Compare the two approaches in a short written note — what SQLAlchemy adds for a larger project.
slots.deliverable: The same real query working through a SQLAlchemy engine, plus a short written comparison against the raw pyodbc version.

lessons.title: Transactions & Error Handling in Database Code

slots.practicalActivity: Wrap a multi-step write (e.g. inserting 3 related rows) in an explicit transaction with commit/rollback, then deliberately trigger a failure partway through (e.g. a bad data type on the 3rd insert) and confirm the rollback actually prevented a partial, inconsistent write.
slots.deliverable: A demonstrated, real rollback: proof (via a verification query) that a failed multi-step write left zero partial rows behind.

slots.practicalActivity: Sketch (in writing) the Extract/Transform/Load design for a pipeline that combines orders.csv with the product-category mapping from Lesson 21, then write the real Extract step: two functions that load each source into its own DataFrame, with basic error handling if either file is missing.
slots.deliverable: A written ETL design note plus two working extract functions (one per real source) with error handling.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a real transform() function that merges the two extracted sources, recomputes line_total, and validates every row against explicit rules (quantity > 0, unit_price > 0, customer_name not null) — rejecting invalid rows into a separate "quarantine" DataFrame instead of silently dropping or keeping them.
slots.deliverable: A transform() function producing both a clean output DataFrame and a quarantine DataFrame of the real rows it rejected, with reasons.

lessons.title: Loading to a Target (File, Database, Warehouse)

slots.practicalActivity: Write a real load() function that writes the clean output from Lesson 29 to both a Parquet file and your staging database table from Lesson 23, and the quarantine rows to a separate quarantine.csv for someone to review by hand.
slots.deliverable: Real output artifacts: a Parquet file, an updated database table, and a quarantine.csv — all produced by one load() function.

slots.practicalActivity: Add a small watermark control table/file tracking the last-processed order_date, then modify your extract step to only pull orders newer than the stored watermark. Run the pipeline twice in a row and confirm the second run correctly processes zero new rows.
slots.deliverable: Proof (via printed row counts) that a second consecutive pipeline run loads zero rows, because the watermark correctly excluded already-processed data.

slots.practicalActivity: Change your Lesson 28 database load to use an upsert (delete-then-insert or MERGE) instead of a plain INSERT, then run the full pipeline twice on the exact same data and confirm the target table has no duplicate rows either time.
slots.deliverable: Proof (via a COUNT(*) query) that running the same load twice produces no duplicate rows in the target table.

slots.practicalActivity: Combine every piece from this chapter (extract, transform/validate, incremental load, idempotent write) into one real, runnable script driven by a small config file (JSON or .env) holding the source paths, database connection details, and watermark location — nothing hardcoded inline.
slots.deliverable: One complete, runnable, config-driven ETL script that performs a full real extract-transform-load run end to end.

lessons.title: Logging in Python (the logging Module)
lessons.chapterTitle: Logging, Testing, Error Handling and Automation

slots.practicalActivity: Replace every print() statement in your Chapter 6 ETL script with proper logging module calls at the right levels (INFO for normal progress, WARNING for quarantined rows, ERROR for failures), writing to both the console and a real log file.
slots.deliverable: Your ETL script running with real logging module output in a log file, at correctly chosen levels.

lessons.title: Writing Unit Tests With pytest
lessons.chapterTitle: Logging, Testing, Error Handling and Automation

slots.practicalActivity: Install pytest and write 3 real unit tests for your Lesson 29 validation function: one proving a valid row passes, one proving a negative-quantity row is correctly rejected, and one proving a null customer_name is correctly rejected. Run pytest and confirm all 3 pass.
slots.deliverable: A test_validation.py file with 3 passing pytest tests, run successfully from the terminal.

lessons.title: Robust Error Handling Patterns
lessons.chapterTitle: Logging, Testing, Error Handling and Automation

slots.practicalActivity: Add a retry pattern (e.g. 3 attempts with a short delay) around your Lesson 17 API call, so a transient network failure doesn't kill the whole script, and log each retry attempt. Simulate a failure by pointing at an invalid URL and confirm the retry-then-fail behavior logs clearly.
slots.deliverable: A retry-wrapped API call that logs each attempt and fails gracefully with a clear message after exhausting retries.

lessons.title: Scheduling & Automating Scripts
lessons.chapterTitle: Logging, Testing, Error Handling and Automation

lessons.title: Environment Variables & Secrets Management
lessons.chapterTitle: Logging, Testing, Error Handling and Automation

slots.practicalActivity: Move your database connection string and API details out of your script into environment variables (using a .env file and python-dotenv), confirm the script still runs correctly reading from them, then write the real OS scheduler command (cron line or Windows Task Scheduler entry) you'd use to run this script nightly at 2 AM.
slots.deliverable: Your ETL script running successfully with zero hardcoded secrets, plus the real cron/Task Scheduler command that would automate it.

slots.practicalActivity: Install PySpark locally, create a SparkSession, and load the course's real NYC Taxi sample data (the same public dataset used in this site's Data Engineering Foundations course) into a Spark DataFrame. Run .show(5) and .printSchema() to confirm it loaded correctly, then filter to trips with a real fare_amount greater than $20.
slots.deliverable: A working local PySpark session that loads the real taxi dataset and correctly filters it by fare amount.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the real taxi dataset, join the trips DataFrame to the zone-lookup DataFrame on location ID, then group by zone and compute the real average fare per zone. Identify, from the actual computed numbers, which zone has the highest average fare.
slots.deliverable: A real, computed average-fare-by-zone result, with the highest-fare zone named from the actual output.

lessons.title: Mini Capstone Part 1: Building the Pipeline

slots.practicalActivity: Build one complete, real PySpark pipeline end to end on the taxi dataset: read the raw data, clean it (drop rows with impossible values like a negative fare or zero passengers), join it to the zone lookup, and compute one real summary metric of your choice (e.g. trips per hour, or revenue per borough).
slots.deliverable: A complete, runnable PySpark script producing one real, defensible summary metric from the cleaned, joined taxi data.

lessons.title: Mini Capstone Part 2: Validating & Presenting Results

slots.practicalActivity: Validate Part 1's result with a sanity check (e.g. does the row count after cleaning make sense relative to the raw count? does the metric's magnitude look plausible?), then write a short, real summary — what the metric shows, how you validated it, and one real data-quality issue you found and handled along the way.
slots.deliverable: A written capstone summary (half a page) covering the real metric, its validation, and one genuine data-quality finding from the real dataset.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can write real, working Python -- functions, files, JSON, and a live public REST API -- then use Pandas to load, clean, and transform real messy data; connect Python directly to a real SQL Server database with pyodbc and SQLAlchemy, including parameterized queries and transactions; build a complete, config-driven, idempotent ETL pipeline with incremental loads and real error recovery; add production practices (logging, pytest unit tests, retries, scheduling, and secrets management); and write and run real PySpark code, closing with a two-part mini capstone that builds and validates a real pipeline against a public dataset.
